USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold the tariffs already in force as leverage but step back from further escalation — specifically, do not push the $200B (List 3) rate from 10% to 25%. Re-engage Beijing in structured talks aimed at protecting our farm and energy exports, using the existing $34B List 1 (and scheduled $16B List 2) duties as a negotiating card rather than a prelude to a broader trade war. The objective is to convert our leverage into concrete Chinese purchase commitments without inflicting self-inflicted damage on the farm belt and consumers.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is material but not existential (threat_score +0.45). China has matched every US tariff dollar-for-dollar — List 1 ($34B) took effect July 6 and China retaliated the same day; List 2 ($16B) was set for Aug 23 with equal Chinese response; and Aug 1's move to consider doubling the $200B list to 25% drew an immediate $60B Chinese retaliation threat (event timeline; Business Insider). The exposure is concentrated in a key export sector: soybeans — ~60% of US ag exports to China — have dropped ~20% since the dispute began, USDA cut its US soybean export forecast ~11%, and farm-belt prices are at levels where many farmers lose money, generating mounting political pressure in Trump's own base (farmpolicynews.illinois.edu; Bloomberg). US consumer sentiment has slipped from 101.4 to 96.2 over five months even as industrial production and the dollar remain strong (UMCSENT; INDPRO; DTWEXBGS, country_health), showing the escalation is already eroding confidence. This warrants a moderate-positive threat reading: real GDP/farm-sector drag and political pressure, but no supply-chain or financial crisis yet. Escalating to 25% on $200B would raise consumer prices, threaten tech supply chains, and deepen the farm-belt wound for uncertain gain, while talks are already at an impasse plagued by mutual distrust (SCMP). The right stance is therefore de-escalation toward negotiation (action_score +0.20, negotiate): keep existing tariffs as leverage, avoid ratcheting to 25%, and seek a deal that locks in agricultural/energy purchases — not a unilateral concession, but a deliberate move to wind down a spiral that is costing more at home than it is extracting from Beijing.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Maintain proportionate, calibrated retaliation that mirrors each U.S. escalation one-for-one (matching the $34B hit, and our announced up-to-25% duties on ~$60B of U.S. goods if Washington proceeds with the $200B List 3), while keeping the negotiation channel explicitly open and avoiding any action that hands Washington pretext to trigger the full $200B at 25%. Do not fire an out-of-proportion first strike, and do not concede structural reform absent a matching U.S. offer.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is high because U.S. actions target the exact sectors of China's economy named in the high-threat anchor: Section 301 tariffs on ~$50B of aerospace/ICT/robotics/machinery (2018-03-22, 04-03 lists), the already-in-force 25% List 1 on ~$34B (07-06), the proposed $200B List 3 raised to 25% (08-01), and the ZTE denial order that set an entity-list precedent against a Chinese tech champion (04-16). Macro confirms strain: the yuan has depreciated ~8% against the dollar this year with its worst four-month fall on record, even though July exports still grew 12.2% and the US surplus stayed near record highs, so the economy has not yet cracked. This is material-but-not-existential, hence +0.55. The action stance is calibrated retaliation (-0.3) rather than maximal escalation or unilateral concession: China's imports from the U.S. are far smaller than its exports, so it physically cannot counter $200B symmetrically, and over-escalating risks provoking the worst-case tariff; but conceding now, before any matching U.S. offer, is politically untenable and would invite further demands. Proportionate mirror-response (which Beijing has already announced) preserves resolve and face while the weakened yuan and front-loaded trade data buy time, and explicitly keeps the door open to talks so we are not the party that closes negotiation.
